question: Can a layer-wise auxiliary-variable training procedure for an arbitrarily deep fully connected network be proved to drive squared training loss to zero outside the neural-tangent-kernel regime, and can a residual/projection variant do so for ReLU networks?

key_findings.claim: For scalar-output regression with no more samples than input dimensions, a full-row-rank data matrix, and a strictly increasing bi-Lipschitz activation, the paper states that its nested gradient-update BCD procedure can make the lifted objective F arbitrarily small.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 5.1 chooses epsilon-dependent outer and inner iteration counts and restrictive step sizes so the output-layer residual contracts while every hidden reconstruction residual is controlled, and reports a soft-O total of nL log^2(1/epsilon) gradient computations. The theorem also requires singular-value-bounded initialization for layers 2 through L and repeated first-layer/auxiliary updates; it is not a guarantee for ordinary end-to-end backpropagation or unconstrained BCD.

key_findings.claim: The claimed optimization theorem is much narrower than the paper's title: the proved main case is scalar-output squared regression under n <= d_in and rank(X) = n, while classification and general multi-output settings are only sketched as extensions.
key_findings.evidence: Section 5 explicitly restricts to d_out = 1. Appendix C says rigorous multi-output convergence is non-trivial, adds a low-rank label assumption, changes the initialization, and proposes importing an asymmetric matrix-factorization theorem. Appendix B calls classification a possible extension but does not supply an integrated convergence theorem.

key_findings.claim: The ReLU result applies to a modified scalar-output residual network with fixed mixed-sign output weights, skip connections, non-negative auxiliary projection, and a first-layer linear update; it is not the same architecture or update rule as the monotone-activation theorem.
key_findings.evidence: Section 6 freezes W_L so every scalar target has a non-negative hidden representation when W_L contains positive and negative entries, an event assigned probability 1 - 2^(1-r) under Gaussian initialization. Theorem 6.3 then states F <= epsilon for Algorithm 3. Algorithm 3 adds residual connections and projections and omits ReLU from the W_1 subproblem.

key_findings.claim: The reported experiments show qualitative loss descent on one synthetic teacher-student regression problem, but they do not test generalization, real data, classification, speed, or accuracy against backpropagation and prior BCD methods.
key_findings.evidence: For n = 500, d_in = 600, width 30, and five repetitions, four-layer LeakyReLU training descends while the no-SVB ablation stalls near 10^-3; depth-8 and depth-12 plots also descend. A four-layer ReLU residual variant descends while the no-skip ablation does not. Only training-loss curves are reported, without numeric final-loss tables or standard optimizer baselines.

key_findings.claim: Theorem 5.5 gives a high-probability Rademacher generalization-gap bound by combining bounded inputs/labels with spectral-norm control of the trained weights, but the bound grows exponentially with depth/width factors and is not empirically evaluated.
key_findings.evidence: The displayed bound contains the network-output scale B_Y + 2^L ell^(L-1) B_X and a capacity term involving (2r)^(L/2), d_in^(1/2), and L^(3/2). The proof substitutes these norm bounds into a prior spectral-normalization lemma; no experiment measures train-test gaps or whether the bound is non-vacuous.

key_findings.claim: The proof of the monotone-activation theorem contains material equation-level gaps as written.
key_findings.evidence: Lemma D.7 defines Delta v = sigma(W V^(0)) - V' but constructs the inverse with sigma(W V^(0)) + Delta v, which targets 2 sigma(W V^(0)) - V' rather than V'; the sign should be reversed for the displayed construction. Lemma D.4 invokes Lemma D.6 to bound weight movement, while Lemma D.6 invokes Lemma D.4 to bound the same weights, without an explicit simultaneous induction. For W_1, the proof uses a positive minimum-eigenvalue contraction for X^T Xi D X although X is n by d_in with d_in >= n, so X^T Xi D X has a nullspace when d_in > n; a row-space invariant could repair this, but it is not established in Lemmas D.10-D.11.

key_findings.claim: The ReLU proof also relies on a projection lemma that is false under its stated assumptions, so Theorem 6.3 is not established by the appendix as written.
key_findings.evidence: Lemma F.3 assumes ||W||_op <= 1/3, V' >= 0, and ||ReLU(WV)+V-V'||^2 <= epsilon, then claims the squared negative part of V is at most epsilon. Its proof additionally asserts V >= 0, which is neither assumed nor true immediately before the projection. Even under the norm bound, the scalar choice W=-1/3, V=-1, V'=0 gives epsilon=4/9 but squared negative part 1, disproving the stated implication. Theorem 6.3 later invokes this lemma after each projection to bound hidden loss.

key_findings.claim: The experimental hyperparameters do not instantiate the sufficient conditions stated in an auditable way.
key_findings.evidence: Sections 7.1-7.2 set all three step sizes to 1 and K_V = K_W = 100 but omit gamma, the outer-iteration count, initialization seeds, and final numeric losses. Theorems 5.1 and 6.3 instead impose small, problem-dependent step-size bounds involving gamma, alpha, data norms, residuals, width, and epsilon, so the plotted runs are empirical demonstrations rather than tests of the theorem's stated regime.

method.core_idea: Lift each hidden representation into a per-example auxiliary variable, penalize disagreement with each layer, and sweep backward through output weights, auxiliary variables, and hidden weights using local gradient steps.
method.mechanism: Algorithm 1 initializes hidden auxiliary variables exactly on the forward pass and clips singular values of layers 2 through L. Each outer iteration updates W_L once, moves V_(L-1) toward the labels, alternates one hidden-weight update with many auxiliary-variable updates from the top down, and performs many W_1 updates. Strict monotonicity makes each square hidden map invertible, while full row rank of X makes per-neuron first-layer interpolation possible. Algorithm 3 replaces hidden maps by residual ReLU maps, projects auxiliary variables non-negative, freezes a mixed-sign scalar output vector, and solves a linear first-layer subproblem.
assumptions: The main theorem treats squared-loss supervised regression with one scalar output.
The data matrix X has rank n and n <= d_in, enabling interpolation at the first layer.
For Algorithm 1, sigma(0)=0, sigma is ell-Lipschitz, and its slope is globally bounded below by alpha>0; standard ReLU, sigmoid, and tanh do not qualify.
All hidden layers have the same square width r, and layers 2 through L begin with singular values clipped to prescribed intervals.
Step sizes and inner/outer iteration counts may depend on data norms, initial residuals, width, depth, gamma, alpha, and target epsilon.
The ReLU theorem uses residual connections, non-negative auxiliary projection, a fixed scalar output vector with both signs, and sufficiently small hidden operator norms.
The Rademacher bound additionally assumes i.i.d. examples and almost-surely bounded inputs and labels.

techniques.role: Replaces the nested network objective by an output residual plus one local consistency penalty per layer and example.
Updates output, auxiliary, and weight blocks from the top layer toward the input so newly moved targets are propagated backward.
Clips square hidden-layer singular values at initialization to preserve invertibility or contraction during the proof.
Uses many auxiliary and first-layer steps but only one update for higher-layer weights to control accumulated drift.
Adds identity skip connections so v -> ReLU(Wv)+v is invertible under an operator-norm contraction condition.
Projects ReLU-side auxiliary representations into the activation range after local gradient updates.
Feeds optimization-derived weight-norm bounds into an existing spectral Rademacher-complexity result.

evaluations.setting: Theorem 5.1: scalar-output depth-L fully connected regression, rank(X)=n<=d_in, strictly increasing bi-Lipschitz activation, SVB initialization, epsilon-dependent nested loops
evaluations.metric: Lifted squared objective F after K outer iterations
evaluations.result: The paper states F <= epsilon for arbitrary epsilon>0 and soft-O(nL log^2(1/epsilon)) gradient computations under its displayed step-size and iteration-count conditions
evaluations.baseline: Prior neural-network BCD guarantees cited by the paper converge to stationary or critical points rather than proving zero training loss

evaluations.setting: Synthetic LeakyReLU teacher-student regression; n=500, d_in=600, four hidden layers, width 30, alpha=0.5, five repetitions
evaluations.metric: Mean training-loss trajectory with standard-deviation band
evaluations.result: The plotted SVB-initialized run decreases monotonically; no numeric final loss is tabulated
evaluations.baseline: Without singular-value bounding, the plotted loss stagnates near 10^-3

evaluations.setting: Same synthetic LeakyReLU task at L=4, 8, and 12
evaluations.result: All three plotted depths decrease, with slower initial descent for deeper networks
evaluations.baseline: Depth is the only comparison; no SGD, backpropagation, MAC, or earlier BCD baseline is run

evaluations.setting: Synthetic ReLU teacher-student regression; n=500, d_in=600, four residual hidden layers, width 30
evaluations.baseline: The no-skip variant fails to converge in the plotted run; architecture and feasible-set mechanics both change

evaluations.setting: Theorem 5.5 under i.i.d. bounded data and the same optimization assumptions
evaluations.result: A spectral Rademacher upper bound is derived with exponential depth/width factors
evaluations.baseline: No numerical bound, held-out error, or competing generalization bound is evaluated

limitations: Author-stated: the main rigorous analysis is for scalar-output squared regression; Appendix C says the multi-output case is non-trivial and needs low-rank labels, altered initialization, and an external matrix-factorization result.

Author-stated: n <= d_in and full row rank are essential to the exact first-layer interpolation argument; when n>d_in the paper only sketches an added residual delta_1 rather than proving the headline theorem.
Author-stated: standard ReLU violates the strictly positive slope assumption, so the ReLU result changes both the architecture and the algorithm and freezes the output layer.
Reviewer-identified: Lemma D.7 has a residual-sign error, Lemmas D.4/D.6 are circular as written, and the W_1 contraction does not state the row-space restriction needed when X^T X is singular.
Reviewer-identified: Lemma F.3's negative-part bound is false without the unstated V>=0 premise, undermining the projection step used in the ReLU theorem.

Reviewer-identified: Appendix B calls logistic/cross-entropy strongly convex, but those losses are not generally strongly convex and separable cross-entropy may have no finite minimizer; the claimed classification extension is therefore not established.
Reviewer-identified: the generalization bound inherits factors exponential in depth and width and is not shown to be non-vacuous.

Reviewer-identified: experiments use only one synthetic interpolation setting, five repeats, and qualitative training-loss plots; they do not measure test error, real-data accuracy, runtime, memory, or comparison with standard and prior BCD optimizers.
Reviewer-identified: gamma, outer-iteration count, random seeds, numeric final losses, and code are not reported in the experimental section, preventing exact reproduction from the paper.
Reviewer-identified: per-example auxiliary variables require O(nLr) storage, and the nested K, K_V, K_W loops may offset the claimed parallelism; no wall-clock evidence is provided.
failure_modes: If n>d_in or X is rank deficient, the first layer cannot generally interpolate arbitrary auxiliary targets and the zero-loss proof stops.
Sigmoid, tanh, standard saturating activations, and any activation with zero derivative violate the global inverse-slope argument.
Hidden weights can lose conditioning if step sizes exceed the proof's accumulated-drift budget, invalidating all later inverse and contraction bounds.
For ReLU, an output vector lacking both positive and negative entries cannot represent arbitrary signed scalar labels with non-negative final auxiliaries.
Projection may increase or otherwise fail to control a hidden residual because Lemma F.3 permits cancellation before projection.
The many local inner steps can be computationally prohibitive on large n, wide networks, or deep models even when blocks are parallelizable.
A tiny lifted loss need not yield a practically competitive classifier or generalizer; the experiments measure interpolation only.
Cross-entropy on separable data can drive weights to infinity rather than attain the finite strongly convex output subproblem assumed in the extension discussion.
reusable_insights: Auxiliary-coordinate lifting can turn a deeply nested objective into local layer-fitting problems that expose exactly where invertibility and rank are needed.
Initialization conditioning can be used as a proof invariant when cumulative block updates are explicitly budgeted.
Different blocks may need deliberately different update counts: a block with fixed full-rank inputs can be solved accurately while moving higher blocks only enough to avoid drift.
Residual maps v -> v + g(v) become invertible when g is a contraction, offering a route around non-invertible activations.

A global-minimum claim should state whether it means convergence of iterates, convergence to a critical point, or objective value approaching the global infimum; prior BCD literature uses 'global convergence' in the first sense.
Equation-level proof audits should test sign conventions, rank dimensions, and circular dependence before treating an epsilon theorem as established.
open_questions: Can Theorem 5.1 be repaired with a non-circular joint induction and an explicit row-space argument, and what constants result?
Is there a valid replacement for Lemma F.3 that controls projection error, or a counterexample to the full ReLU algorithm?
Can exact global convergence be proved for multi-output classification without low-rank labels and without assuming a finite strongly convex cross-entropy minimizer?
How does the method compare in wall time, memory, test accuracy, and sensitivity against backpropagation, MAC, proximal BCD, and KL-based alternating minimization on real datasets?
Are the epsilon-dependent theoretical step sizes large enough to produce useful convergence in finite precision?
Can mini-batch or stochastic block updates retain any zero-loss or population-risk guarantee while removing O(nLr) auxiliary storage?
When is the stated Rademacher bound numerically non-vacuous as depth and width grow?

competitive_landscape.title: Distributed optimization of deeply nested systems
competitive_landscape.relationship: Foundational direct predecessor for auxiliary-coordinate training of deep nested models.
competitive_landscape.difference: MAC already introduces one auxiliary coordinate per layer and example and alternates parameter and coordinate optimization with parallelism and convergence analysis. The present paper specializes a quadratic-penalty gradient sweep and claims objective convergence to zero under stronger rank, activation, and conditioning assumptions.
competitive_landscape.source_version: PMLR volume 33, AISTATS 2014, pages 10-19 (official proceedings final)

competitive_landscape.title: Convergent Block Coordinate Descent for Training Tikhonov Regularized Deep Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct prior BCD method for lifted ReLU networks.
competitive_landscape.difference: Zhang and Brand lift ReLU into a smooth multiconvex Tikhonov-regularized formulation and claim R-linear convergence to a stationary point, with MNIST comparisons to SGD variants. The present work removes proximal/Tikhonov updates and targets arbitrarily small loss, but only after changing the ReLU architecture and under restrictive interpolation assumptions.

competitive_landscape.title: Lifted Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Askari et al. encode non-decreasing activations as convex argmin penalties so block steps become shallow supervised problems and emphasize initialization and robustness. The present paper instead uses squared consistency penalties and a strict inverse-slope condition to claim zero lifted loss.

competitive_landscape.title: A Proximal Block Coordinate Descent Algorithm for Deep Neural Network Training
competitive_landscape.difference: Lau et al. use proximal BCD and a Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz analysis to obtain global convergence of the iterate sequence and report standard-dataset comparisons. The present paper uses vanilla local gradient steps and seeks the stronger zero-training-loss conclusion, but supplies much narrower synthetic evidence.

competitive_landscape.title: Global Convergence of Block Coordinate Descent in Deep Learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest prior convergence framework spanning common DNN splitting schemes and ResNets.
competitive_landscape.difference: Zeng et al. prove convergence to critical points at O(1/k) for two- and three-splitting BCD models under KL-style conditions and cover general smooth losses and ResNets. The present paper's novelty is specifically convergence of objective value to zero/global infimum, not the broader phrase 'global convergence.'
competitive_landscape.source_version: PMLR volume 97, ICML 2019, pages 7313-7323 (official proceedings final)

competitive_landscape.title: A block coordinate descent optimizer for classification problems exploiting convexity
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct layer-block alternative for neural-network classification.
competitive_landscape.difference: Patel et al. alternate a globally optimized convex cross-entropy output layer with gradient-trained hidden layers and evaluate dense and convolutional classifiers. The present paper updates every layer through auxiliaries and proves a scalar squared-regression interpolation result; its classification discussion is not a proved or tested counterpart.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims the first BCD guarantee that an arbitrary-depth neural network reaches global minima/arbitrarily small loss outside NTK assumptions, plus a ReLU extension and a Rademacher generalization bound.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The official primary competitors establish auxiliary-coordinate formulations, lifted/multiconvex BCD, proximal/KL convergence, convergence to critical points, or output-layer convex optimization, but their advertised guarantees do not establish zero loss for the same arbitrary-depth lifted objective. Theorem 5.1 is therefore a distinct target on paper.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The potentially new contribution is the attempted zero-objective contraction proof for a specially initialized, scalar-output, overparameterized interpolation regime, not BCD, lifting, parallel auxiliary variables, ResNet splitting, or 'global convergence' broadly. Material sign, circularity, rank-subspace, and ReLU-projection defects mean the strongest theorem is not established by v1 as written. The empirical contribution is only a synthetic feasibility illustration and does not support practical or generalization superiority.

reviewer_notes: Primary full-text review covered all 32 pages of arXiv:2510.22667v1: main assumptions and algorithms, both headline theorems, all synthetic figures, Algorithms 2-3, extension discussions, the complete proofs in Appendices D-F, and the depth study in Appendix G. The indexed PDF pin was independently checked on 2026-08-23 by downloading https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.22667v1; its SHA-256 exactly matched 023e6520607e857f6f07fb0b2911c61aebb44a2d6fb26b865c8a78d50a3ff77c. The local extract covers 32/32 pages. Equation audits were checked visually against PDF page 19 for the Lemma D.7 sign, not inferred from OCR alone. Six exact official primary competitor records were opened and version-pinned on 2026-08-23. Confidence is high in the scope and documented contradictions, but slightly below maximal because this is a primary rather than independent formal peer-verification pass.
